title: Al-Idrisi and the Map of the World
summary: How the scholar al-Idrisi gathered and checked reports from travelers to make one of the most accurate world maps of the Middle Ages for King Roger of Sicily.
poll: Asking many people is a better way to learn about a place than reading one book.

versions.title: The Man Who Mapped the World
versions.text:
Maps help us find our way. Long ago, good maps were rare. One man set out to fix this. His name was al-Idrisi.

He was born in North Africa. That was near the year 1100. He was a scholar. He liked to read and learn. He went to school in Spain. Then he took long trips.

A king named Roger ruled Sicily. He sent for the man. He wanted a map of the world.

The man did not guess. Ships came to the port. He spoke to each traveler. He spoke to sailors too. Each one had things to tell. He wrote down what they said. Did lots of them say the same thing? Then he kept that fact.

His book told of towns and hills. It told of roads, too. It told how far each town was.

It was a big job. The work took 15 years. It was done in 1154. He made a big silver map. His book had 70 small maps.

Look at his map. South is at the top! He knew the Earth is round. The map shows the land of Arabia. It shows Makkah and Madinah.

The silver map was lost. But we still have copies of the book.

He was born in North Africa, close to the year 1100. He was a scholar. He loved to learn. He went to school in a big city in Spain. Then he went on long trips to see new lands.

A king named Roger ruled the island of Sicily. He asked the young man to come and work for him. The king wanted a map of the whole world.

The man did not just guess. Ships came to the port each day. He spoke to each traveler. He spoke to sailors, too. He wrote down what they told him. He kept a fact only if lots of them said the same thing.

His book told about towns, rivers, hills, and roads. It told how many days it took to get from one town to the next.

The work took about 15 years. It was done in 1154. He made a huge map on a disc of silver. He wrote a book, too. It had 70 small maps.

On his map, south is at the top! He knew that the Earth is round. The map shows the land of Arabia, with Makkah and Madinah.

Sad to say, the silver map was lost. But people made copies of his book. You can see them in libraries now.

versions.title: Al-Idrisi and His Map of the World
versions.text:
Long ago, good maps were hard to find. Most people knew very little about lands far away. One man set out to make the best map of the world. His name was al-Idrisi.

He was born in North Africa around the year 1100. He was a scholar. He loved to learn. He studied in Cordoba, a great city in Spain. When he was young, he went on long trips.

A king named Roger ruled the island of Sicily. He asked al-Idrisi to come and work for him. The king wanted a map that showed the whole world.

Al-Idrisi did not just guess. Ships came to the busy port each day. He met each traveler who came. He asked sailors and traders what they had seen. He wrote down what they said. He kept a fact only when many of them agreed.

His book told about towns, rivers, mountains, and roads. It also told how many days it took to go from one town to the next.

The work took about 15 years. At last, in 1154, it was done. He made a huge map on a disc of silver. He also wrote a book with 70 small maps inside.

To us, his map looks upside down. South is at the top! He also knew that the Earth is round. The map even shows the land of Arabia. You can find Makkah and Madinah on it.

Sadly, the silver map was lost long ago. But people copied his book by hand. You can still see those copies in libraries today.

versions.title: Al-Idrisi and the Map of the World
versions.text:
About nine hundred years ago, reliable maps were rare, and most people possessed little knowledge about distant lands beyond their own region. One remarkable scholar set out to change that situation by creating the most accurate map of the world produced in his era. His name was al-Idrisi.

Al-Idrisi was born around the year 1100 in a town in North Africa and studied in Cordoba, a celebrated center of learning in Spain. As a young man, he traveled extensively, and he eventually became an accomplished cartographer, a specialist who designs and draws maps.

Roger the Second, the king of the island of Sicily, invited al-Idrisi to his court because he desired a map that displayed every region of the known world in detail.

Rather than simply reproducing older maps, al-Idrisi interviewed travelers, sailors, and merchants who arrived at the island's busy ports. He compared their reports carefully and tried to verify each fact, accepting it only when several independent witnesses agreed. Descriptions that contradicted each other were excluded.

The project required approximately 15 years and was completed in 1154. Al-Idrisi produced an enormous map engraved on a disc of silver, and he also composed a book that divided the known world into seven climate zones, each separated into ten sections, for a total of 70 detailed maps.

For each section, his book described towns, rivers, mountains, and roads in remarkable detail, and it explained how many days of travel separated one town from the next.

To modern readers, the map appears upside down, because its orientation places south at the top. Al-Idrisi also understood that the Earth is round. His map even includes the Arabian Peninsula, with the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah clearly marked.

Unfortunately, the silver map disappeared long ago. However, scribes copied his book by hand, and several of those manuscripts survive in libraries today.

For centuries afterward, scholars in both the Islamic world and Europe studied his work. His careful method of gathering many accounts and trusting only those that agreed resembles the way modern researchers check their sources.

versions.title: Al-Idrisi and the Map of the World
versions.text:
About nine hundred years ago, reliable maps were exceptionally scarce, and most people possessed little knowledge about distant territories beyond their immediate region. One remarkable scholar set out to transform that situation by creating the most comprehensive and accurate representation of the world produced in his era. His name was al-Idrisi.

Al-Idrisi was born around the year 1100 in a town in North Africa and studied in Cordoba, a celebrated center of learning in Spain. As a young man, he traveled extensively, and he eventually became an accomplished cartographer, a specialist who designs and draws maps.

Roger the Second, the king of the Mediterranean island of Sicily, invited al-Idrisi to his court because he desired a map that displayed every region of the known world in considerable detail.

Rather than simply reproducing older maps, al-Idrisi systematically interviewed travelers, sailors, and merchants who arrived at the island's bustling ports. He compared their reports meticulously and attempted to verify each fact, accepting information only when several independent witnesses agreed. Descriptions that contradicted each other were deliberately excluded.

The ambitious project required approximately 15 years and was completed in 1154. Al-Idrisi produced an enormous map engraved on a disc of silver, and he also composed an accompanying book that divided the known world into seven climate zones, each subdivided into ten sections, for a total of 70 detailed regional maps.

For each section, his book described towns, rivers, mountain ranges, and trade routes in remarkable detail, and it specified how many days of travel separated one settlement from the next, information that proved invaluable to merchants and pilgrims alike.

To contemporary readers, the map appears upside down, because its orientation places south at the top, a convention shared by numerous mapmakers of his civilization. Al-Idrisi also understood that the Earth is spherical. His map also includes the Arabian Peninsula, with the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah clearly identified.

Unfortunately, the silver map disappeared centuries ago; however, scribes meticulously copied his book by hand, and several of those manuscripts survive in libraries today.

For centuries afterward, scholars throughout both the Islamic world and Europe consulted his work extensively, and his rigorous method of gathering numerous independent accounts and trusting only those that corroborated one another closely resembles the procedures that contemporary historians and scientists employ when evaluating the reliability of their sources.

It told them which towns had silver.
It showed them which kings to obey.

questions.stem: What can you infer about al-Idrisi's view of a single traveler's story?
options: He thought it was always correct.

wrong.A: Then he would not have checked it against others.

HIGH.prompt: Al-Idrisi trusted information only when several independent sources agreed. Explain how you could use the same method to check a fact you read online today.
checklist: I explained al-Idrisi's method using details from the article.
I applied the method to a modern example.
I used at least two key words correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Al-Idrisi, a careful cartographer, refused to trust a single traveler's account; instead, he gathered reports from many sailors and merchants and only recorded a fact once several independent sources agreed on it. I could use this same method to verify a surprising claim I read online today by searching for two or three other trustworthy websites and checking whether they report the same information. If only one source makes the claim and nothing else confirms it, I would treat it the way al-Idrisi treated an unconfirmed story, as something not yet proven. Just as his caution kept errors out of the manuscripts that preserved his work, cross-checking several sources today helps keep false information out of what I believe.
